newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's Stals sees status quo on rates for now.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's Stals sees status quo on rates for now.

text.p: September money supply data showed some stabilisation in the rate of M3 and credit extension growth, and implied the maintenance of the status quo on interest rates for now, Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals said.
"It confirms that we maintain the status quo for the time being," Stals told Reuters in a telephone interview on Monday.
"It confirms that there has been a levelling off in the rate of increase in the last few months," he said of the figures released late on Friday.
"We are looking for indications that it will come down to a lower rate of increase but at least it is encouraging that the rate it is not increasing further."
Broadly defined M3 money supply grew a better-than-expected 14.45 percent in September, down from 15.40 in August, but private credit extension disappointed, expanding by 17.94 percent from 17.70.
Stals had warned in a speech on Friday that already high interest rates might have to be raised further if there was no slowdown in money supply and credit growth.
Commenting on the current account deficit -- another major headache for the central bank -- Stals said he expected little improvement in calendar 1996 compared to 1995.
"The total deficit last year was 12-1/2 billion rand, more or less. It will probably be of that same order (this year), maybe a little bit smaller...I would say around about 12 billion rand."
The deficit on the current account of the balance of payments stood at 6.9 billion rand for the six months to June 30, 1996, compared to 12.7 billion in calendar 1995.
But there were signs the tide was starting to turn and Stals said he expected the gap to narrow further from now on.
"There is a good chance that the fourth quarter deficit will be smaller than the third quarter. I think we are at last beginning to see the effects on the current account."
The current account would be helped by a slowdown in gross domestic expenditure, the sharp depreciation in the rand since February and the increasing effect of tight domestic financial conditions.
Stals said he had been surprised by the market's negative reaction to his comments on Friday which saw the rand fall through 4.60 against the dollar for the first time.
"If we do things to control bank credit extension and money supply it must help the balance of payments and it must help the exchange rate," he said.
"I'm a bit surprised if we say that we will do the necessary things to support the balance of payments and bring it back into equilibrium that the reaction is negative in the foreign exchange rate."
The Reserve Bank had intervened heavily in the foreign exchange market on Friday but the pressure on the currency had eased on Monday.
"On Friday there was quite heavy intervention. This morning it is much less and it looks like the market is stabilising again today," Stals said.

He declined to comment on the effect of intervention on official reserves, but said the central bank had not been very active in the market prior to Friday and the country had not drawn further on overseas credit lines.
South Africa borrowed 612 million rand in September to bolster its reserves which stood at just 10 billion rand at Setptember 30, equivalent to four weeks import cover.
-- Ben Hirschler, Johannesburg newsroom +27 11 482 1003
